idiom_name: hand-rolled memo table: calloc'd per-rule array of input_length+1 cells, or an open-addressing table
implementation_notes: C has neither a map type nor generics, so the memo table is the part you write yourself: with positions bounded by the input length, the simplest correct table is one row per rule of n+1 cells allocated with calloc and addressed as memo[rule * ncols + pos], where each cell records the rule's outcome - a result struct or an explicit FAIL state - so a recorded failure is reused instead of retried. What replaces the classic structure is that the uniform accessor plus a rule table of function pointers (cell_t (*rules[])(struct parser *, size_t pos)) is the whole pattern; the table travels in a parser context rather than in a file-scope global, so two parses or two threads cannot share it. The classic memo object with its own lifecycle is justified exactly when the parser is a reusable module with several entry points; for a single-shot parse, calloc around one entry call and free afterwards is enough. There is no packrat support in the C standard library, which is why the level is manual rather than library.
pitfalls: Sizing: a static or fixed-capacity table either overflows on a longer input or silently serves stale cells - columns must come from the actual input length (len + 1) and rows from the rule count, and the block is freed when the parse ends.

A void*-style memo cell loses the type the parser stored in it: a cell read under the wrong tag is undefined behaviour the compiler cannot check, so keep the tag/state in the cell and cast only under a matching tag.
A file-scope memo makes the parser non-reentrant: two inputs, or two threads, sharing one table get cross-contaminated results that still look deterministic.
